description: We’re Sumukh, Priti and Tejas, a team passionate about space, engineering, physics, and technology. We bring skills in aerospace, astronomy, coding, physics, and computer science. We aim to build a creative, competitive NASA Space Apps project and seek teammates skilled in coding, data, design, and research.
summary:
Vector Mars Maps is an interactive Mars navigation tool to help prospective astronauts to calculate safer, quicker routes on Mars. Our team is leveraging NASA Mars data, such as Mars Trek images and elevation data, to calculate the shortest distance and terrain-aware route between points of interest, such as Perseverance Landing, the Western Delta and the Western Breach.

We constructed a 10,000-node terrain grid, and then used Dijkstra's algorithm to generate routes optimized for distance, elevation change, slope and uphill travel. The terrain-aware route discourages the use of steeper and more challenging terrain, enabling users to assess the relative safety of a route compared to its total distance. The web tool also shows route statistics and information about locations and science.

This solves the problem by putting NASA's mapping and terrain data to use in a navigational system that could guide astronauts toward safer routes without sacrificing their ability to reach points of high science value.
details:
An interactive system for planning safer routes on Jezero Crater. With the application, you will set a starting point and destination, and choose between two routes: one that minimizes the distance traveled and another that minimizes uphill travel, slope, and elevation change between set points.

We mapped the terrain data onto a 100 × 100 grid and created links between neighboring points on the grid to generate a graph. For each link, we calculated the distance traveled, the difference in elevation, and the resulting slope. We used Dijkstra's routing algorithm to calculate routes for Perseverance Landing, the Western Delta, and the Western Breach in terrain-aware mode, which penalizes ascending slopes and slope magnitude above a prototype threshold.

A key advantage of this project is that the route planning does not automatically assume that the quickest route is the most optimal. For instance, compared to the Western Delta–Western Breach route, the terrain-aware route had very similar total travel distance, but greatly lowered maximum slope and total uphill travel. This illustrates that planning routes can lead to safer and more energy-efficient travel.

Route statistics (distance, total vertical distance traveled, total downhill distance traveled, maximum slope of any segment, comparison to Mars Trek profile distances) are also included. Destination info will tell you the scientific and geographic context of each mission destination.

Natural viewer NASA Mars Trek imagery and elevation data, terrain processing, calibration, graph building, routing Python Blender to visually check and validate terrain model and route geometry HTML, CSS, and Javascript to build the interactive web application Run locally with VS Code, published to a publicly accessible internet site using GitHub Pages

What's innovative about the project is that it uses planetary science data, along with pathfinding algorithms and an interactive mission planning UI. Rather than just creating a Mars data visualization as a map, it leverages the existing map data to make route decisions that can be acted upon. We weighed route distance, elevation, slope, astronaut effort, scientific destination value, map accuracy, validation against NASA Mars Trek data.

The goal is to show how the next generations of Mars exploration technology could blend NASA data sets and artificial intelligence routing to get explorers to interesting science locations while minimizing dangerous terrain and physical strain.
